items.description: Branner Earth Sciences Library & Map Collection Exhibit: Water in the West Our Fall 2026 exhibition highlights the water resources in California & the Western United States to shed light on the issues that affect our waterways. The exhibit features maps and the Layperson’s guides series published by the Water Education Foundation, which aim to foster public understanding of water resources. These resources help inform collaborative decision-making to build collective solutions for water issues across the Western United States.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: This Room Holds the World: 500 Years of Prints from the Humanities Art Collection
items.description: San José State Special Collections & Archives is proud to present the first major exhibit of rare art prints from The Humanities Art Collection. The Humanities Art Collection consists of original art prints that were purchased for research and reference use for the study of art and humanities at San José State University. The artworks in this collection were bought for the Humanities Reading Room (also called the Art Reading Room) for reference use in the Wahlquist Library.

items.title: California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: This Room Holds the World: 500 Years of Prints from the Humanities Art Collection
items.description: San José State Special Collections & Archives is proud to present the first major exhibit of rare art prints from The Humanities Art Collection. The Humanities Art Collection consists of original art prints that were purchased for research and reference use for the study of art and humanities at San José State University. The artworks in this collection were bought for the Humanities Reading Room (also called the Art Reading Room) for reference use in the Wahlquist Library.

items.title: California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century.

items.title: Geophysics Master's Presentation, Hamad Alswaidan: "Machine Learning-Assisted Full Waveform Inversion: Low-Frequency Extrapolation and Cycle-Skipping Mitigation
items.description: Full waveform inversion (FWI) is a powerful technique for estimating subsurface physical properties from seismic data. However, its nonlinear nature and the limited availability of low-frequency seismic data make it susceptible to cycle skipping, often preventing convergence toward an accurate subsurface model. In this work, Hamad explores two complementary machine learning approaches to address these challenges. The first investigates the use of generative diffusion models to extrapolate missing low-frequency content in seismic data.

items.description: Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Emerging Technologies and Strategic Stability
items.description: About the event: Emerging technologies developed since the end of the Cold War—and their proliferation to new actors—call into question the prospects for strategic stability in the twenty-first century. Strategic stability exists when rivals are mutually deterred and lack any rational incentive to escalate to nuclear use during conflict. Yet emerging technologies—with their new knowledge and tools with the potential for enhancing military capabilities—are impacting stability in such ways that the assumptions of rationality and deterrence no longer hold.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Jana Hunter- The Child of Freedom: Temporal Sovereignty in Habsburg Bohemia
items.description: Who decides what time it is? In Habsburg Bohemia, that question drew in nearly every other: nation and empire, identity and sovereignty, capital and a newly connected world. Railways and telegraphs created a time shared across distance, and with it a debate over who had the power to set it. Histories of time standardization have told a story of unification; histories of Habsburg sovereignty, meanwhile, have located its conflicts in diets and parliaments.

How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century.

items.title: Emergent Properties: Decennial Reflections on Collections
items.description: In 2026 the David Rumsey Map Center celebrates its tenth year—a moment to reflect on how the Center has added value to scholarship on campus and around the world. Our collections are vast and not bounded by geography, spanning the 15th century to the present. Yet over the last decade, certain materials have repeatedly resonated with the students, instructors, and researchers who frequent the Center.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Tangling the Digital: Weaving, Printmaking, Computing
items.description: Digital objects are often seen as alien to craft, as though no hands had shaped them. They can be copied endlessly and exactly, bereft of the maker’s touch. Yet weaving and printmaking are among our oldest technologies of reproduction, fixing patterns so they can be repeated and circulated. The printing press and the Jacquard loom initiated processes of automation that displaced human hands—and that still animate our digital tools. Warp and weft describe not just a textile structure but a logic of making, where two distinct threads cross, hold, and pull against each other.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.title: Autumn Quarter: End-Quarter Period
California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

items.description: San José State Special Collections & Archives is proud to present the first major exhibit of rare art prints from The Humanities Art Collection. The Humanities Art Collection consists of original art prints that were purchased for research and reference use for the study of art and humanities at San José State University. items.title: Autumn Quarter: End-Quarter Period
California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: California Current: Art and Histories from the Bay Area
items.description: How does a community stay rooted in a region that’s constantly changing? California Current invites you to consider this question and others through its more than 60 works — many on view for the first time — that explore the interplay between Bay Area history, art, and artists over the past century. Titled after the major cold-water current that runs the length of the West Coast of North America, California Current brings together paintings, sculptures, works on paper, photographs, and time-based media by Bay Area artists from the twentieth century to the present.

items.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
items.description: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions.

items.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
items.description: Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery.

items.title: Korean Indigenous Futures: The Art of Kim Bong-Jun 김봉준 판화전: 토착적 미래- K아트, 디아스포라, 세계
items.description: The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future.

items.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
items.description: Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France.

items.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
items.description: Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day.

items.title: 2026 Neurotrauma Symposium
items.description: This one-day symposium brings together leading experts in neurotrauma to deliver cutting-edge insights into the contemporary management of traumatic brain injury (TBI) and spinal cord injury (SCI). Designed for a multidisciplinary audience, the program integrates translational research, clinical innovation, and patient-centered care to optimize outcomes in acute neurotrauma. Participants will explore the latest evidence in rapid SCI alerting systems, surgical decompression, intraspinal pressure monitoring with lumbar drains, and autoregulation assessment using bedside maneuvers.

items.description: Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century.

items.title: A Vision of Paris: The Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford
items.description: Stanford University Libraries presents A Vision of Paris: the Roxane Debuisson Collection at Stanford, on view in the Peterson Gallery and Munger Rotunda of the Cecil H. Green Library from September 22, 2026 to January 24, 2027. Roxane Debuisson (1927–2018) dedicated sixty years to documenting the transformation of the city of Paris during the nineteenth century. If Roxane Debuisson could not stop the changes she saw underway in the late 20th century, she could at least preserve the city’s earlier history through images, literature, guidebooks, and other documents.

Many of the works on view are being presented for the first time. Founded in 2018 by Stanford art history professor Marci Kwon and Cantor associate curator of modern and contemporary art Aleesa Pitchamarn Alexander, the AAAI is one of the nation's leading museum initiatives dedicated to Asian American art.

items.title: Patty Chang: surfacing

Chang’s multimedia sculptural practice brings together archaeological remains from Point Alones Chinese Fishing Village (now the site of Stanford’s Hopkins Marine Station), fish specimens from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology, and archival materials documenting the lives of Chinese fisher families on the Monterey Peninsula.

items.title: Detecting adaptive and ghost introgression in human populations using machine learning approaches
items.description: It is now widely recognized that introgression from archaic humans left a lasting impact on the modern human genome, yet many questions remain unanswered regarding how introgressed variants contributed to adaptation and whether additional, unsampled archaic hominins also contributed to the modern human gene pool. In this talk, I will present recent works from my lab to study both adaptive and ghost introgression in humans. First, I will discuss a work on adaptive introgression in modern Peruvian populations.

items.title: Chinese Railroad Workers, Leland and Jane Stanford, and the Founding of the University
items.description: The completion of the first transcontinental railroad in 1869 connected the East and West coasts of the United States. It was a dramatic engineering, social, economic, and cultural development and hailed as a great national accomplishment. Thousands of workers from China made it possible. Their contribution has been underappreciated and even forgotten. Stanford Professor Gordon Chang will draw on his years of scholarship to recover the story of the Chinese Railroad Workers, their surprising relationship to the Stanfords, and their important place in the early University.

items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. items.title: Something Sensational to Read: A Tour of Silicon Valley LGBTQ+ Publications, 1950 to Today
items.description: September 15–December 16, 2026 SJSU Special Collections and Archives’ new exhibit explores over 70 years of dialogue within LGBTQ+ community publications about daily life, group concerns, and political actions in San José, Santa Clara County, and the greater Bay Area. Spanning unique and obscure self-published works to nationally circulating publications, this massive collection of newspapers, magazines, event programs, organization newsletters, periodicals, and reference materials illustrates the events that shaped, defined, and changed the last near-century of LGBTQ+ history.

The artworks in this collection were bought for the Humanities Reading Room (also called the Art Reading Room) for reference use in the Wahlquist Library.
